title: Vegetable Fajitas
subtitle: Charred peppers, courgette, and mushrooms in warm flour tortillas
excerpt: A mixture of peppers, courgette, mushrooms, and red onion cooked with cumin, smoked paprika, and lime until charred and deeply flavoured, served in warm flour tortillas with soured cream and guacamole.
sourceNotes: Vegetable fajitas: a meat-free adaptation of the classic Tex-Mex fajita, replacing the protein with a mix of charred vegetables. Became a standard American restaurant option from the 1990s, and is one of the better vegetarian adaptations of a meat-origin dish because the char and spice profile carries without needing a protein substitute.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The vegetables can be cooked up to 2 hours ahead and reheated briefly in a hot pan. Add a squeeze of lime before serving.

content.text: Vegetable fajitas work when the vegetables are properly charred rather than just cooked. A pan at medium-high heat and minimal stirring are the key: leave the vegetables alone long enough to develop colour on each side. Courgette (zucchini) and mushrooms release a lot of moisture; they need space in the pan and consistent high heat to drive off liquid and brown rather than steam.

items.prepNote: juice only, plus wedges to serve
mashed with lime juice and salt

content.text: Cook in batches if the pan is crowded. A single large layer of vegetables chars properly; a double layer steams.
Mix the cumin, smoked paprika, chilli powder, lime juice, and olive oil. Toss all the vegetables in this mixture to coat.

Heat a wide frying pan over medium-high heat until very hot. Add the red onion and cook for 3 minutes without stirring. Add the peppers. Cook for 4-5 minutes, turning once or twice, until charred at the edges.

Add the courgette and mushrooms. Turn the heat to high. Cook for 4-5 minutes more, stirring once, until the courgette has colour and the mushrooms are cooked through and the pan looks dry. Add {{garlic}} of crushed garlic for the final minute. Season with salt.
Serve the vegetables straight from the pan in warm flour tortillas with soured cream, mashed avocado, coriander, and lime wedges.

items.symptom: Vegetables are wet and grey, not charred
items.cause: Pan overcrowded or heat too low
items.fix: Cook in batches if needed. A crowded pan drops temperature and the vegetables steam. High heat and space are more important than keeping everything in one go.

items.cause: Added at the same time as the peppers and overcooked
items.fix: Add the courgette and mushrooms after the peppers, not with them. They need less time and go soft quickly. 4-5 minutes maximum for courgette.

items.cause: Spices didn't cook in, or lime juice missing
items.fix: Make sure the garlic goes in at the end with a minute of cooking. The lime juice at the start helps the spices adhere; a squeeze of fresh lime at the end brightens the whole dish.

items.cause: Too much liquid in the vegetable filling
items.fix: Cook the filling until the pan is dry. Drain any pooled liquid before serving. Serve immediately; don't let assembled fajitas sit.

content.text: Vegetable fajitas became a standard US restaurant dish from the late 1980s, when Tex-Mex menus began including vegetarian options. They work as a dish in their own right when the vegetables get the same high-heat treatment as the beef in the original. The char, the spice, and the lime are what make a fajita.
